checks.prompt: Four requirements arrive. (a) A brand wants its founder's voice on marketing videos, cloned from a short recording with consent, at the highest naturalness available. (b) A regulated bank must synthesise millions of statement summaries with audio never leaving its own infrastructure. (c) A hobbyist wants speech on a battery-powered device in a shed with no network. (d) A product team wants a live voice agent that responds in well under a second. Which does this platform fit, and what disqualifies it from the others?
checks.explanation: The trade this platform makes is money and a network round trip in exchange for top-tier quality and no machine-learning operations. That fits work where naturalness sells the result and fits real-time agents, because a dedicated low-latency model exists for exactly that. It does not fit a strict data-residency requirement or an offline device, because synthesis happens on the provider's hardware — and per-character billing is what makes very high volume the wrong shape for it, which is where a self-hosted or on-device engine belongs.
options: (a) and (d): it is the naturalness benchmark with easy cloning, and its lowest-latency model targets real-time conversation. (b) is disqualified because everything is hosted — audio leaves the machine and billing is per character, which both scale badly for millions of items under residency rules. (c) is disqualified for the same hosted reason plus the need for a network, which an offline embedded engine solves instead

(a) and (b): its enterprise tier runs inside your own infrastructure, and the per-character price makes bulk work cheap; the live agent case needs a self-hosted model because a network round trip is always too slow
(c) and (d): the platform's small on-device runtime covers the shed and the low-latency agent, while cloning and bulk statement work belong to self-hosted toolkits
All four: since the models run on the provider's hardware, none of the requirements interact with where the audio goes or how much text is pushed through

checks.prompt: Describe this platform with the vending-machine analogy and name the three orthogonal knobs a request carries, saying what each one decides and where it appears in the call. Explain why keeping them separate matters — give a concrete example of changing one without the others. Then say what you never touch, and what you pay for.
checks.expected: A correct answer must set up the analogy: you do not own or run the model — you supply a key, choose a voice and a model, feed in text, and audio comes back, billed by how much text you pushed through. The three knobs must be named and distinguished. The voice identifier decides WHO speaks — the timbre and identity — and can be a stock voice, one added from the shared library, or your own clone; it addresses the request. The model identifier decides how good and how fast: a top-quality multilingual model, a balanced one, an ultra-low-latency one intended for conversational agents, and a most-expressive one supporting inline delivery tags — this is the quality-versus-latency dial. The delivery settings decide HOW the chosen voice performs: how consistent versus expressive it is, how tightly it adheres to the source voice, how exaggerated the style is, and whether extra fidelity to the source is applied. Orthogonality must be illustrated: the same voice can be switched from the quality model to the low-latency model with no change of identity, or made calmer or more expressive without changing either the voice or the model. What you never touch must be stated — weights, vocoders, sample rates beyond choosing an output encoding — and what you pay for is characters of text, at a rate that depends on which model you chose. Noting that the same key and the same voices are shared across the surrounding products — cloning, re-voicing, dubbing, speech recognition, agents — is a plus.

checks.prompt: A narration project sounds flat and lifeless. Someone proposes raising the consistency setting to its maximum, reasoning that higher is better. A colleague adds that the character voices in the same project wobble and occasionally mispronounce words, and proposes lowering it for those. Evaluate both proposals, and say what the right fix is for an unusual surname the model keeps mangling.
checks.explanation: The consistency control is a genuine trade rather than a quality dial: turn it up and delivery is steady but flatter; turn it down and it is expressive but can wobble and mispronounce. So flat narration wants it LOWER and wobbling character work wants it HIGHER — both proposals push the wrong way. Pronunciation of unusual names, jargon and acronyms is a different problem with its own tool: a pronunciation dictionary carrying phonetic rules or aliases, which is structured and reviewable, unlike deliberately misspelling words in the text.
options: Neither direction is universally 'better': that setting is a trade — high gives consistency at the cost of sounding flat, low gives expressiveness at the cost of wobbling and occasional mispronunciation. So raising it for flat narration is the wrong direction, and lowering it for wobbling character work is also the wrong direction; each should move toward the other. The surname is a separate problem entirely, and the structured fix is a pronunciation dictionary supplying phonetic rules or an alias, rather than misspelling the word to trick the model
Higher is better in both cases: consistency improves pronunciation as well as steadiness, so raising it fixes the flatness, the wobble and the surname together

The setting only affects multilingual models, so neither proposal applies; the flatness and the wobble are both properties of the chosen voice, and the surname requires cloning a speaker who says it correctly
Both proposals are right as stated, and the surname should be handled by respelling it phonetically in the input text, which is the documented approach

checks.prompt: Model the request contract and the cost arithmetic — nothing is sent. Define `RATE` mapping `"eleven_multilingual_v2"` and `"eleven_v3"` to 1.0 and `"eleven_turbo_v2_5"` and `"eleven_flash_v2_5"` to 0.5; `PLAN_CREDITS` mapping `free`, `starter`, `creator`, `pro` and `scale` to 10000, 30000, 100000, 500000 and 2000000; `ACCEPT` mapping the format families `mp3`, `pcm` and `ulaw` to `"audio/mpeg"`, `"audio/pcm"` and `"audio/basic"`; `MAX_REQUEST_CHARS = 5000`; and `BASE = "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech"`. Write `credits(text, model_id)` returning the character count times that model's rate, raising `ValueError` for an unknown model, and `fits_plan(text, model_id, plan)` returning whether that cost is within the plan's quota, raising `ValueError` for an unknown plan. Write `chunk_text(text, limit=MAX_REQUEST_CHARS)` splitting on whitespace and greedily packing words back together with single spaces so that no chunk exceeds `limit`, returning a list (empty for empty input) and raising `ValueError` if any single word is longer than the limit. Write `build_request(voice_id, text, model_id, voice_settings=None, output_format="mp3_44100_128", api_key="$ELEVENLABS_API_KEY")` returning `{"method": "POST", "url", "headers", "body"}`, where the url is the base, a slash, the voice id and `?output_format=<format>`; the headers carry the key under `"xi-api-key"`, a JSON content type, and the accept type for the format's family (the part before the first underscore); and the body carries the text, the model id and the settings, defaulting to stability 0.5, similarity boost 0.75, style 0.0 and speaker boost True with any supplied values overriding. Raise `ValueError` for an unknown model, for text longer than `MAX_REQUEST_CHARS` (the message mentioning chunks), for an unknown format family, and for any of the three numeric settings outside 0 to 1 inclusive. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The arithmetic at the top is the estimate worth doing before pushing a script, and it makes the real lever visible: the same text on a half-rate model costs half as much, which is a bigger effect than any setting on the request. Note the pair of plan assertions where identical text fits on one model and not the other. The chunking block encodes a limit people meet late — one request cannot carry a whole book — and the assertion after it is the point worth remembering: splitting the work changes the number of requests, not the bill, so it is retries and regenerations that cost money, not chunk count. The request itself shows the three knobs living in three different places: identity in the path, quality and latency in the body's model, delivery in the settings, and the encoding in both the query string and the accept header. And a setting outside its range is refused rather than silently clamped, because a clamped value would quietly produce a performance you did not ask for.
checks.test:
script = "Welcome to the show. " * 50
script = script.strip()
assert len(script) == 1049, len(script)

# Billing is per character, and the faster models bill at half rate -- which is the
# lever that actually moves a large bill, not any setting on the request.
assert credits(script, "eleven_multilingual_v2") == 1049.0
assert credits(script, "eleven_v3") == 1049.0
assert credits(script, "eleven_flash_v2_5") == 524.5
assert credits(script, "eleven_turbo_v2_5") == 524.5
assert credits("", "eleven_v3") == 0.0
try:
    credits("hi", "eleven_ultra_v9")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unknown model must be refused")

assert fits_plan(script, "eleven_multilingual_v2", "free") is True
assert fits_plan("x" * 10_001, "eleven_multilingual_v2", "free") is False
# ...and the same text on a half-rate model fits where the full-rate one does not.
assert fits_plan("x" * 15_000, "eleven_multilingual_v2", "free") is False
assert fits_plan("x" * 15_000, "eleven_flash_v2_5", "free") is True
assert fits_plan("x" * 15_000, "eleven_multilingual_v2", "starter") is True
assert fits_plan("x" * 40_000, "eleven_multilingual_v2", "starter") is False
assert fits_plan("x" * 40_000, "eleven_flash_v2_5", "starter") is True
try:
    fits_plan("hi", "eleven_v3", "enterprise")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unknown plan must be refused")

# A long script cannot be sent as one request, so it is packed into chunks that fit.
chunks = chunk_text(script, limit=200)
assert all(len(c) <= 200 for c in chunks), [len(c) for c in chunks]
assert " ".join(chunks) == " ".join(script.split()), "the text must survive chunking"
assert len(chunks) > 1
# Packing is greedy, so adding the next word would have overflowed each chunk.
for index, chunk in enumerate(chunks[:-1]):
    first_of_next = chunks[index + 1].split()[0]
    assert len(chunk) + 1 + len(first_of_next) > 200, (index, chunk)
assert chunk_text("", limit=10) == []
assert chunk_text("one two three", limit=100) == ["one two three"]
assert chunk_text("aaa bbb ccc", limit=7) == ["aaa bbb", "ccc"]
try:
    chunk_text("supercalifragilistic", limit=5)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("a word longer than the limit must be refused")

# Chunking changes the number of requests, not the bill: the characters are the same.
assert sum(credits(c, "eleven_v3") for c in chunks) + (len(chunks) - 1) == \
    credits(" ".join(script.split()), "eleven_v3")

request = build_request("21m00Tcm4TlvDq8ikWAM", "Hello there.",
                        "eleven_multilingual_v2")
assert request["method"] == "POST"
assert request["url"] == ("https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/"
                          "21m00Tcm4TlvDq8ikWAM?output_format=mp3_44100_128")
assert request["headers"]["xi-api-key"] == "$ELEVENLABS_API_KEY"
assert request["headers"]["Content-Type"] == "application/json"
assert request["body"]["model_id"] == "eleven_multilingual_v2"
assert request["body"]["text"] == "Hello there."

# The three knobs are independent: identity is the path, quality and latency are the
# model in the body, and delivery is the settings.
assert "21m00Tcm4TlvDq8ikWAM" in request["url"]
assert request["body"]["voice_settings"] == {
    "stability": 0.5, "similarity_boost": 0.75, "style": 0.0,
    "use_speaker_boost": True}
tuned = build_request("v1", "hi", "eleven_flash_v2_5",
                      voice_settings={"stability": 0.2})
assert tuned["body"]["voice_settings"]["stability"] == 0.2
assert tuned["body"]["voice_settings"]["similarity_boost"] == 0.75
assert tuned["body"]["model_id"] == "eleven_flash_v2_5"
assert "v1" in tuned["url"]

# The declared format decides what the server is asked to return.
assert build_request("v1", "hi", "eleven_v3",
                     output_format="pcm_24000")["headers"]["Accept"] == "audio/pcm"
assert build_request("v1", "hi", "eleven_v3",
                     output_format="ulaw_8000")["headers"]["Accept"] == "audio/basic"
assert "output_format=ulaw_8000" in build_request(
    "v1", "hi", "eleven_v3", output_format="ulaw_8000")["url"]
for bad in ("flac_44100", "wav", "opus_48000"):
    try:
        build_request("v1", "hi", "eleven_v3", output_format=bad)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad!r} must be refused")

# Settings are fractions; a value outside the range is a caller error, not a clamp.
for setting in ({"stability": 1.5}, {"similarity_boost": -0.1}, {"style": 2.0}):
    try:
        build_request("v1", "hi", "eleven_v3", voice_settings=setting)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{setting} must be refused")

# One request cannot carry a whole book; the chunks it was split into all can.
try:
    build_request("v1", "x" * (MAX_REQUEST_CHARS + 1), "eleven_v3")
except ValueError as exc:
    assert "chunks" in str(exc), exc
else:
    raise AssertionError("an over-long request must be refused")
long_script = " ".join(["word"] * 4000)
for chunk in chunk_text(long_script):
    build_request("v1", chunk, "eleven_v3")

checks.prompt: A batch narration job goes wrong in three ways: parallelising it produces a burst of rejected requests; a regression test comparing audio byte-for-byte against last month's recording now fails; and a telephony integration receives audio the phone system cannot play. What explains each?
checks.explanation: Three independent facts about using a hosted service. Concurrency is capped per plan, so a batch job that fans out hits rejections and needs throttling and backoff rather than more parallelism. Determinism is best-effort — the model is hosted and can be updated underneath you — so byte-for-byte comparison is the wrong test; pin the model identifier, use a seed if offered, and judge output perceptually. And the output encoding has to match the consumer: telephony wants a specific low-rate format, further signal processing wants raw samples, and the web wants the compressed default.
options: Each plan caps how many requests may run at once, so parallelising past that cap produces rejections — throttle and back off rather than fanning out. The audio is not reproducible byte-for-byte: it is a hosted model whose output can vary between runs and change when the provider updates a version, so pin the model identifier, use a seed where one is offered, and test perceptually rather than by bytes. And the telephony failure is the output encoding: phone systems want a specific low-rate telephony format, not the default compressed one
The rejections mean the account ran out of credits mid-job, which is also why the audio changed — a fallback voice was substituted; and the telephony problem is that streaming was not enabled
All three are version drift: pinning the model identifier restores the concurrency limit, the byte-identical output and the telephony encoding together

The rejections are a network problem best solved by retrying immediately; the changed audio means the delivery settings were not sent, so defaults were applied; and the telephony system needs the highest-quality format available

checks.prompt: Compare this platform against the big cloud vendors' speech services, an open self-hosted cloning toolkit, and a tiny on-device engine. For each, say what it wins on and what it costs. Then advise a company producing 500 hours of audiobook narration a year in one branded voice, who also want an in-app assistant that speaks responses on mid-range phones with patchy connectivity. Say what you would use where, and what you would check before committing.
checks.expected: A correct answer must position all three alternatives. The big cloud vendors win on enterprise scale, service guarantees, rich speech markup, huge voice catalogues and compliance posture, at the cost of generally being less natural and expressive and requiring more configuration — and they are still paid, hosted services. The open self-hosted cloning toolkit wins on running on your own hardware with no per-use bill and on training or cloning your own voices, at the cost of running the infrastructure yourself, quality that trails, and community rather than vendor maintenance. The tiny on-device engine wins on running in real time offline on modest hardware with no cost and no network, at the cost of lower naturalness, no cloning, and minimal prosody control. The recommendation must split the two workloads. Narration is where naturalness sells the product and where the branded cloned voice matters, so this platform fits — but the answer must engage with cost, since 500 hours is a very large number of characters and per-character billing accumulates, so estimating the annual credit spend against plan quotas, and considering the half-rate faster models where quality suffices, is part of the advice; batching also has to respect the per-request length limit and the plan's concurrency cap. The in-app assistant on mid-range phones with patchy connectivity should NOT depend on a hosted service for its speech — an on-device engine is the right answer there, since it works with no network and costs nothing per use. Things to check before committing must include: consent and terms for the cloned voice, whether output determinism matters given that the hosted model can change between versions, data residency for the audio being sent, and the output formats available on the intended plan. Noting that the two paths can coexist — the brand voice for produced content, a local engine for interactive speech — is a plus.
